gov-policy.summary: A short, Board-approved set of rules (policy) and detailed how-tos (standards) that say what everyone must do to keep information safe.
gov-policy.protects: The whole estate indirectly: it makes every control enforceable, auditable and fundable; without it, misconduct and audit findings cannot be acted on.
gov-policy.placement: Process, owned by the CISO; approved by the Board or its IT Strategy / Risk committee; published on the intranet and acknowledged by staff.
gov-policy.how: One top-level information security policy sets intent and roles. Topic standards (access, data, cloud, vendors, incidents) set measurable rules. Each is reviewed at least yearly and after major change, and exceptions go through a tracked process.
pareto: One top policy plus about 10-12 standards, not 60 documents
Formal approval and yearly review recorded in Board or committee minutes
Staff acknowledgement each year, tied to induction and awareness training
Every rule maps to a control someone owns and can show evidence for
An exception route with an end date, so rules bend visibly, not silently

gov-privacy.summary: The programme that makes the organisation meet India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and DPDP Rules 2025: lawful notice and consent, security, breach reporting and people's rights.
gov-privacy.protects: Personal data of customers and staff; protects the organisation from penalties of up to Rs 250 crore per breach category and from loss of trust.
gov-privacy.placement: Process owned by a Data Protection Officer (DPO) or privacy lead with the CISO and Legal; touches every system that holds personal data; consent and rights handled in customer channels.
gov-privacy.how: Map what personal data is held, why, where and with whom. Give a plain notice and take consent (or rely on a listed legitimate use). Protect it (Rule 6: encryption or masking, access control, logs, backups), report breaches to the Data Protection Board and affected people, keep logs for at least one year, honour rights, and bind processors by contract. Status at October 2026: the Rules were notified on 13-14 November 2025; Board provisions apply now; consent-manager registration starts about 13 November 2026; most duties (notice, consent, security, breach reporting, retention, children's data, rights) and penalties apply from about 13 May 2027. A January 2026 MeitY proposal to shorten this to 12 months had not been notified as of early October 2026; watch the Gazette.
pareto: Personal data map and processing register, by system and purpose
Notice and consent flows fixed in the top customer journeys
Breach process: notify the Board without delay, full report within 72 hours; tell affected people in plain words
Processor contracts with security, breach and deletion terms
Rights and grievance desk with tracked response times

gov-iso27001.summary: An information security management system (ISMS) certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 by an accredited certification body.
gov-iso27001.protects: The durability of all controls: an audited yearly cycle keeps them alive; also wins customer and regulator trust.

gov-iso27001.how: Define scope, assess risks, choose controls in a Statement of Applicability (93 Annex A controls in the 2022 version), run them, audit internally and review with management. An accredited body does a two-stage certification audit, then surveillance audits in years 2 and 3 and recertification in year 3.

gov-grc.summary: Software that keeps policies, risks, controls, audits, vendors and exceptions in one place, with evidence.
gov-grc.protects: Governance efficiency and audit readiness; stops spreadsheets drifting and evidence going missing.

gov-insurance.summary: An insurance policy that pays for the money impact of a cyber incident: response costs, business interruption, data restoration, liability and regulatory defence.
gov-insurance.protects: The balance sheet against the residual cost of a major incident (ransomware, breach, fraud).
gov-insurance.placement: Process owned by the CFO with the CISO and Legal; bought through a licensed broker; claims run with the incident response team.
gov-insurance.how: Size the limit to a realistic worst case from the risk register. The insurer underwrites on a questionnaire about controls (MFA, backups, EDR, patching). Premium is a percentage of sum insured, adjusted for sector and posture. In a claim the insurer's panel (forensics, legal) often joins the response.
pareto: Right limit from a worst-case scenario, not a round number
MFA, EDR, offline backups and patching proven (they drive premium and claim success)
Check exclusions: war and state actors, unpatched systems, contractual liability, regulatory fines
Know the notification clause and the insurer's panel before an incident

gov-ai.summary: Rules and checks for how the organisation buys, builds and uses AI, so it is safe, fair, lawful and under human control.
gov-ai.protects: Customers and the organisation against wrong or biased decisions, data leakage into AI tools, prompt injection and model misuse, and regulatory breach.
gov-ai.placement: Process owned by the CISO with the CRO and a model-risk owner; AI inventory in the GRC tool; technical guardrails at the AI gateway.
gov-ai.how: Keep an inventory of every AI use and rate each by impact. Approve uses against a Board-approved AI policy, test models before use (accuracy, bias, security) and monitor them in production. A human stays accountable for decisions that affect customers. In India: RBI's FREE-AI framework (13 Aug 2025) recommends a Board-approved AI policy for regulated entities, and MeitY's India AI Governance Guidelines (5 Nov 2025) set seven principles and rely on existing laws (IT Act, DPDP) rather than a new AI statute. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 gives a certifiable management system.
pareto: An inventory of all AI uses, including staff use of public chat tools
A Board-approved AI policy with risk tiers
Pre-use testing and approval for high-impact uses
Data rules: what may and may not go into AI tools
AI terms in vendor contracts (data use, bias, audit)

prc-inventory.summary: A complete, current list of every device, system, application, cloud service and data store, with its owner and what it holds.
prc-inventory.protects: Everything else: unknown assets are unpatched, unmonitored and unprotected; the inventory is the base for patching, monitoring, DPDP mapping and continuity.
prc-inventory.placement: Process owned by IT with the CISO; discovery agents or scanners on the network and endpoints; a CMDB or asset register in the ITSM tool.
prc-inventory.how: Discovery tools find devices, software and cloud resources automatically. Each item gets an owner, a classification and a business service. The list is reconciled monthly against other sources (EDR, directory, cloud accounts, purchase records) to catch gaps.
pareto: Automated discovery of endpoints, servers and cloud accounts
An owner and a business service for each of the 40 applications
Internet-facing assets listed and checked weekly
Monthly reconciliation of EDR, directory and CMDB counts
Data stores with personal or sensitive data flagged

prc-classify.summary: Rating every asset for how critical it is to the business and how sensitive its data is, so effort follows importance.
prc-classify.protects: Sensitive and personal data and critical services: classification decides where encryption, DLP, backups, monitoring and access rules apply first.
prc-classify.placement: Process owned by business owners with the CISO; ratings kept in the asset inventory; data labels applied in email, documents and storage by a labelling tool.
prc-classify.how: Each asset gets two scores, criticality and sensitivity (1-4 each, for example Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted). The product sets its priority. Documents and email carry visible labels, applied by default or suggested by content detection, so tools such as DLP can act on them.
pareto: Four simple levels, defined with examples
Business owners rate their own systems
Default labels in email and Office documents, user can raise
Automatic detection of personal data (Aadhaar, PAN, account numbers) to suggest labels
Labels drive DLP and encryption rules

prc-change.summary: A controlled way to make changes to systems and to grant temporary exceptions to rules, so nothing risky goes in unreviewed and no 'temporary' exception lasts forever.
prc-change.protects: Availability and integrity of systems; stops outages from bad changes and quiet holes from forgotten exceptions.
prc-change.placement: Process owned by IT (change manager) with the CISO; run in the ITSM tool; change advisory board for high-risk changes; exceptions in the GRC register.
prc-change.how: Each change is logged with a risk rating, test evidence and a back-out plan; standard low-risk changes are pre-approved, high-risk ones go to the change board. Each exception has an owner, a reason, a compensating control and an end date, and is reviewed before it expires.
pareto: Every production change logged and linked to an approval
Pre-approved standard changes to keep speed
Emergency change route with review after the fact
Exceptions with end date and compensating control
Compare changes found by monitoring with changes approved (catch unauthorised ones)
